analysis.one_liner: Shield vaccine and drug makers from lawsuits over emergency medicines, making the federal government the only defendant.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: after being sent to two House committees and a Health subcommittee in October 2005, it never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for lawsuits over drugs, vaccines, and devices used against pandemics, epidemics, or bioterror attacks. Instead of suing the manufacturer, an injured person would have to sue the United States government, and manufacturers could only be held liable if the Attorney General personally found, by clear and convincing evidence, that they willfully broke safety laws and caused the injury. The bill never moved past its initial referrals to committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturers, distributors, and health care providers who dispense emergency countermeasures. If a pandemic vaccine or drug injured someone, they could not be sued directly; judgments would be paid by the federal government, and the company itself would face liability only in the rare case of an Attorney General determination of willful misconduct.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an exclusive federal cause of action so that all claims over pandemic or epidemic products and security countermeasures are brought solely against the United States, not the manufacturer, distributor, or health care provider [S2] [S3].

Sets a rebuttable presumption of immunity for the government — and effectively for companies — covering stockpile products and any product the HHS Secretary designates for a public health emergency [S2] [S3].

A company can be sued only if the Attorney General finds clear and convincing evidence of an intentional or willful violation of drug-safety laws that created a significant health risk and caused the injury — a much higher bar than a normal negligence lawsuit [S2] [S3].

The Attorney General's decision on whether to even investigate an injured party's petition cannot be reviewed by any court, and only the company can appeal an adverse determination — injured people are barred from intervening in that appeal [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would fund judgments against the federal government for injuries caused by manufacturers' products, and injured people, who would lose the ordinary right to sue the company that made or sold the product and face a single federal court in Washington, D.C. as their only forum.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and people injured by emergency products

drawbacks.text: The bill routes all injury claims to the federal government and bars suits against manufacturers unless the Attorney General makes a rare willful-misconduct finding that is largely outside judicial control, leaving injured people with little practical recourse against the company responsible [S2] [S3].

The strongest good-faith argument for the bill is that manufacturers may decline to develop unproven pandemic vaccines and drugs if a single jury verdict could bankrupt them, so some liability protection may be needed to keep emergency products on the market; this bill, however, would also apply to FDA-approved products sold during designated emergencies, a much broader shield than the narrow development-risk problem it addresses [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument that some liability protection is needed to get companies to make emergency countermeasures, but this bill goes far beyond that: it shifts the cost of virtually all product injuries during a declared emergency onto taxpayers, funnels every case through one court, and makes holding a company accountable dependent on a single discretionary decision by the Attorney General that courts cannot review. For ordinary people, the protections come at the price of both recourse and public money.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in October 2005 and referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees, then to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa introduced the bill on October 6, 2005, with two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat [S1] [S4] [S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].
On October 17, 2005, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; no further action was recorded for the remainder of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who could have been injured by an emergency vaccine or drug keep the ordinary ability to hold manufacturers accountable, and taxpayers avoid funding manufacturer liability. Drug and vaccine makers gain nothing from this particular bill, though a narrower federal liability shield for countermeasures was enacted separately in December 2005, so the industry did not leave the year empty-handed (general historical context, not from the provided sources).

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured people kept their day in court

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to establish liability protections for pandemic and countermeasure products.

for.name: Two House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Referring committee; its Health Subcommittee held the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Referring committee with jurisdiction over the liability provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only cosponsors were one Republican and one Democrat, so it had nominal bipartisan support, but no votes were ever taken and no recorded opposition exists in the record — the bill simply never advanced out of committee.

industries.note: The bill would make manufacturers essentially immune from lawsuits over pandemic and epidemic products, with the federal government standing in as the sole defendant and taxpayer funds paying any judgments. Their gain is the public's loss of recourse when a product causes harm.

industries.industry: Drug distributors and health care providers
industries.note: Distributors, administrators, and providers who dispense designated countermeasures would also be shielded from direct suits, so patients injured by dispensing errors or administration would have to look to the federal government instead.
